How Sparse Attention Approximates Exact Attention?
Your Attention is Naturally nCn^{C}-Sparse

Yichuan Deng ††thanks: ycdeng@cs.washington.edu. The University of Washington.    Zhao Song ††thanks: magic.linuxkde@gmail.com. Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing, University of California, Berkeley.    Jing Xiong ††thanks: junexiong@connect.hku.hk. The University of Hong Kong    Chiwun Yang ††thanks: christiannyang37@gmail.com. Sun Yat-sen University.

Sparse Attention is a technique that approximates standard attention computation with sub-quadratic complexity. This is achieved by selectively ignoring smaller entries in the attention matrix during the softmax function computation. Variations of this technique, such as pruning KV cache, sparsity-based fast attention, and Sparse Transformer, have been extensively utilized for efficient Large Language Models (LLMs) deployment. Despite its widespread use, a theoretical understanding of the conditions under which sparse attention performs on par with traditional attention remains elusive. This work aims to bridge this gap by examining the inherent sparsity of standard attention processes. Our theoretical framework reveals several brand-new key insights:

  • •

    Attention is nCn^{C}-sparse, implying that considering only the largest Ω⁡(nC)\Omega(n^{C}) entries out of all nn entries is sufficient for sparse attention to approximate the exact attention matrix with decreasing loss. Here, nn represents the input length and C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1) is a constant.

  • •

    Stable o⁡(log⁡(n))o(\log(n))-sparse attention, which approximates attention computation with log⁡(n)\log(n) or fewer entries, may not be feasible since the error will persist at a minimum of O⁡(1)O(1).

  • •

    An adaptive strategy (α⋅nC,α∈ℝ\alpha\cdot n^{C},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}) for the window size of efficient attention methods rather than a fixed one is guaranteed to perform more accurately and efficiently in a task for inference on flexible context lengths.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) [VSP+17, RNS+18, DCLT18, RWC+19, BMR+20, CND+22, ZRG+22, Cha22] have emerged as a cornerstone of contemporary artificial intelligence, exhibiting remarkable capabilities across a plethora of AI domains. Their prowess is grounded in their ability to comprehend and generate human language with a level of sophistication that is unprecedented. This has catalyzed transformative applications in natural language processing, including machine translation [HWL21], content creation [Cha22, Ope23], and beyond, underscoring the profound impact of LLMs on the field of AI.

However, the architectural backbone of these models, particularly those built on the transformer framework [VSP+17], presents a significant challenge: computational efficiency [TDBM22]. The essence of the transformer architecture, the Attention mechanism, necessitates a computational and memory complexity of O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), where nn represents the sequence length. This quadratic dependency limits the scalability of LLMs, especially as we venture into processing longer sequences or expanding model capacities.

In an effort to mitigate this bottleneck, the AI research community has pivoted towards innovative solutions, one of which is sparse attention [CGRS19, CNM19]. Sparse attention mechanisms aim to approximate the results of the full attention computation by selectively focusing on a subset of the input data points. This is typically achieved by omitting certain interactions in the Query and Key multiplications within the attention mechanism, thereby inducing sparsity in the attention matrix. In order to arrive at the goal of preserving the model’s performance while alleviating the computational and memory demands, prior works, including pruning KV cache, sparsity-based fast attention, and sparse transformer modeling, demonstrate outstanding efficiencies with O⁡(n1+o⁡(1))O(n^{1+o(1)}) (sub-quadratic) complexity and sub-linear memory cache with competitive performance compared with standard attention across various tasks [LWD+23, ZSZ+24, KMZ23, ALSY23, LLS24, XZC+21, ZHDK23, AS23, AS24b, AS24a, HJK+23].

Despite these advancements, the theoretical underpinnings of sparse attention mechanisms and their implications on model performance and behavior remain an area of active inquiry. In detail, it’s not clear when and when not sparse attention can approximate standard attention with a stable error. Also, the sparsity that attention naturally processes, which we call attention sparsity, lacks a strict confirmation of its existence and measurement. Especially, we would like to ask:

How Sparse Attention Approximates Exact Attention?

Our Contributions. In this work, we explore the theory of the sparse attention computation problem. Particularly, we first provide a analysis framework that first theoretically confirms the sparsity appears in standard attention. In detailed, our analysis describes the relationships between attention sparsity and input boundary, weights of attention networks and context length. Therefore, we derive several incremental insights based on this framework. In summary,

  • •

    We estimate the lower bound on the requirement for (ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparse softmax vector, proving the vanilla attention computation is naturally sparse (see Section 4).

  • •

    We introduce the concept of attention collapse, which demonstrates the number of effective entries in attention matrix provably decrease to 11 or some constant inevitably. (see Section 5)

  • •

    We give the sufficient lower bound on the window size of stable sparse attention approximating exact attention computation, Ω⁡(nC)\Omega(n^{C}) for constant C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1). This further indicates that sparse attention can recover attention outputs from limited Ω⁡(nC)\Omega(n^{C}) entries while achieving a decreasing error. (see Section 6.1)

  • •

    Meanwhile, we also confirm sparse attention approximation from o⁡(log⁡(n))o(\log(n)) entries is not enough for stability and extensibility since the lower bound on error will grow with increasing input length. (see Section 6.2)

  • •

    Therefore, we suggest to use adaptive strategy k=α⋅nC,α>0,C∈(0,1)k=\alpha\cdot n^{C},\alpha>0,C\in(0,1) for the window size of sparse attention rather than the strategy that fixes the window size for any input. The former is proved more efficient within higher approximation performance. (see Section 7)

2 Related Work

Sparse and Efficient Transformer.

In the landscape of attention mechanisms, Vaswani et al. introduced the transformative transformer model, revolutionizing NLP with its comprehensive self-attention mechanism [VSP+17]. Innovations [CGRS19, LSR+19] in sparse attention presented methods to reduce complexity, maintaining essential contextual information while improving computational efficiency. The Reformer [KKL20] utilized Locality Sensitive Hashing to significantly cut down computational demands, enabling the processing of lengthy sequences. Mongoose [CLP+20] adapted sparsity patterns dynamically, optimizing computation without losing robustness. [SYY21] introduced a learning-to-hash strategy to generate sparse attention patterns, enhancing data-driven efficiency. HyperAttention [HJK+23] refined attention approximation, balancing computational savings with accuracy. Longformer [BPC20] extended transformer capabilities to longer texts through a mix of global and local attention mechanisms. The Performe [CLD+20] offered a novel approximation of softmax attention, reducing memory usage for long sequences. Big Bird [ZGD+20] combined global, local, and random attention strategies to surmount traditional transformer limitations regarding sequence length.

Theoretical Approaches to Understanding LLMs.

There have been notable advancements in the field of regression models, particularly with the exploration of diverse activation functions, aiding in the comprehension and optimization of these models. The study of over-parameterized neural networks, focusing on exponential and hyperbolic activation functions, has shed light on their convergence traits and computational benefits [BSZ23, SWY23, GSY23, DMS23a, GSX23, SYZ23, ZHDK23, AS23, AS24b, AS24a, GSWY23, DSXY23, LSWY23, CSY24]. Enhancements in this area include the addition of regularization components and the innovation of algorithms like the convergent approximation Newton method to improve performance [LSZ23]. Additionally, employing tensor methods to simplify regression models has facilitated in-depth analyses concerning Lipschitz constants and time complexity [GSX23, DLMS23]. Concurrently, there’s a burgeoning interest in optimization algorithms specifically crafted for LLMs, with block gradient estimators being utilized for vast optimization challenges, significantly reducing computational load [CLMY21]. Novel methods such as Direct Preference Optimization are revolutionizing the tuning of LLMs by using human preference data, circumventing the need for traditional reward models [RSM+23]. Progress in second-order optimizers is also notable, offering more leniency in convergence proofs by relaxing the usual Lipschitz Hessian assumptions [LLH+23]. Moreover, a series of studies focus on the intricacies of fine-tuning [MGN+23, MWY+23, PSZA23]. These theoretical developments collectively push the boundaries of our understanding and optimization of LLMs, introducing new solutions to tackle challenges like the non-strict Hessian Lipschitz conditions.

3 Preliminary

In this section, we formalize the problem we strive to address, along with the definitions, and assumptions that underpin our work. Especially, Section 3.1 explains the main theory of the problem we aim to study. In Section 3.2, we give a unified definition of the sparsity-based attention method and how it approximates exact attention computation, and we call it sparse attention.

Assumption. In this work, we consider one-layer self-attention computation both in standard form and sparsity-based approximate form. To begin with, we give the assumption of the input matrix of attention computation, denoted as X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} where nn is the context length and dd stands the dimension, as follows (refer to Definition C.1 for the formal and detailed version of assumption):

  • •

    Independent Entries. For any two entries Xi1,j1X_{i_{1},j_{1}} and Xi2,j2X_{i_{2},j_{2}} in matrix XX, ∀i1,i2∈[n]\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in[n] and j1,j2∈[d]j_{1},j_{2}\in[d], they are independent.

  • •

    Bounded Entries. For failure probability δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). With a probability 1−δ1-\delta, the entry Xi,jX_{i,j} in matrix XX, ∀i∈[n]\forall i\in[n] and j∈[d]j\in[d], we have |Xi,j|≤B|X_{i,j}|\leq B for some positive constant B>0B>0.

Attention Computation. Hence, we are about to introduce the standard attention computation, which occupies the main time and space complexity O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) in LLMs inference. First, we denote the weights of query, key and value projection as WQ,WK,WV∈ℝd×dW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Thus, we let query, key and value state matrices be computed by Q:=X​WQ,K:=X​WK,V:=X​WV∈ℝn×dQ:=XW_{Q},K:=XW_{K},V:=XW_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. We state the following definition:

Definition 3.1 (Attention computation).

Given Query, Key and Value states matrices Q,K,V∈ℝn×dQ,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. We then define A:=exp⁡(Q​K⊤/d)A:=\exp(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d}), D:=diag⁡(A​𝟏n)∈ℝn×nD:=\diag(A{\bf 1}_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. The attention computation 𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V)∈ℝn×d{\sf Attn}(Q,K,V)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is given by:

𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V):=D−1​A​V∈ℝn×d\displaystyle{\sf Attn}(Q,K,V):=D^{-1}AV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}

Specially, we denote D−1=diag⁡(1/(A​𝟏n))∈ℝn×nD^{-1}=\diag(1/(A{\bf 1}_{n}))\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

3.1 Attention Sparsity

In Definition 3.1, D−1​A∈ℝn×nD^{-1}A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} represents the attention matrix, indicating how much the model focuses on each vector. In much of the sparse attention literature, D−1​AD^{-1}A is assumed to be sufficiently sparse, allowing sparsity-based efficient attention methods to disregard some zero entries in order to achieve a balance between accuracy and efficiency. In this paper, we introduce a threshold, denoted as ϵ\epsilon, and define attention sparsity as the number of entries in each row of D−1​A∈ℝnD^{-1}A\in\mathbb{R}^{n} that are smaller than ϵ\epsilon. Specifically, for a softmax vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, if there are at least n−kn-k entries in uu that are not greater than ϵ\epsilon for all integers k∈[n]k\in[n], we say that uu is (ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparse. Since ϵ\epsilon is intended to be a very small value, we will simply refer to uu as being kk-sparse. The formal definition is provided below:

Definition 3.2 ((ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparsity).

For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and error ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we define sparse set 𝒮ϵ​(u)\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u) as: 𝒮ϵ​(u):={i∈[n]||ui|≤ϵ}\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u):=\{i\in[n]~|~|u_{i}|\leq\epsilon\}. Hence, we say uu is at least (ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparse when it holds that |𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥n−k.|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq n-k.

Problem Definition I: Estimating ϵ\epsilon. In practical implementations, establishing a clear relationship between ϵ\epsilon and the sparsity kk proves to be challenging. Therefore, we first analyze how to estimate a boundary for ϵ\epsilon based on a given sparsity integer k∈[n]k\in[n]. Naively, given kk, we would like to find a guaranteed value for ϵ\epsilon that satisfies |𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥n−k|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq n-k. Addression this problem will enable us to assess the loss associated with approximating standard attention using sparse attention, ultimately guiding us in finding the optimal trade-off between ϵ\epsilon (where lower values yield greater accuracy) and kk (where lower values lead to higher efficiency).

3.2 Sparse Attention and Approximation

Here we state an ideal mathematical definition for the sparse attention in this paper. Initially, we define a set, 𝒯k​(u){\cal T}_{k}(u), to filter out the greatest kk entries in a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. The integer k∈[1,n]k\in[1,n] is also called window size in some sparse attention works.

Definition 3.3.

For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, given a sparsity integer kk, we denote a top-kk set 𝒯k​(u):={i∈[n]|𝒮ui​(u)≥n−k}{\cal T}_{k}(u):=\{i\in[n]~|~{\cal S}_{u_{i}}(u)\geq n-k\}, then we define vector

𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(u):=[u1⋅𝟏1∈𝒯k​(u),⋯,un⋅𝟏n∈𝒯k​(u)]⊤∈ℝn.\displaystyle{\sf topk}(u):=[u_{1}\cdot{\bf 1}_{1\in{\cal T}_{k}(u)},\cdots,u_{n}\cdot{\bf 1}_{n\in{\cal T}_{k}(u)}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Note that 𝟏i∈𝒯k​(u){\bf 1}_{i\in{\cal T}_{k}(u)} is an indicator where when i∈𝒯k​(u)i\in{\cal T}_{k}(u), it equals 11, otherwise, 00. We utilize 𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(u){\sf topk}(u) to compute a sparsity-based approximating version of A=exp⁡(Q​K⊤)A=\exp(QK^{\top}) in Definition 3.1, we denote it AsparA_{\rm spar}. Accordingly, we provide a universal version for all sparsity-based attention as follows:

Definition 3.4 (Sparse attention).

Given Query, Key and Value state matrices Q,K,V∈ℝn×dQ,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. We then define A:=exp⁡(Q​K⊤/d)∈ℝn×nA:=\exp(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Especially, we define Aspar:=[𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(A1,∗),⋯,𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(An,∗)]⊤A_{\rm spar}:=\begin{bmatrix}{\sf topk}(A_{1,*}),\cdots,{\sf topk}(A_{n,*})\end{bmatrix}^{\top}, Dspar:=diag⁡(Aspar​𝟏n)∈ℝn×nD_{\rm spar}:=\diag(A_{\rm spar}{\bf 1}_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. The sparse attention computation 𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V)∈ℝn×d{\sf SparseAttn}(Q,K,V)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is given by:

𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V):=Dspar−1​Aspar​V∈ℝn×d\displaystyle{\sf SparseAttn}(Q,K,V):=D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}

Specially, we denote Dspar−1=diag⁡(1/(Aspar​𝟏n))∈ℝn×nD_{\rm spar}^{-1}=\diag(1/(A_{\rm spar}{\bf 1}_{n}))\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

It should be noted that directly accessing top k entries in the attention matrix without any extra computational cost is overly ideal for efficient LLMs in real-world cases. Prior works usually utilize some additional approximate algorithm to meet this condition, e.g. Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) for retrieving larger query-key pairs, but this also brings more approximating errors. We only focus on the part of approximating attention computation in this study and leave the part of pre-approximating top-k entries in D−1​AD^{-1}A as a future direction.

Problem Definition II: Sparse Attention Approximation. The variations of sparse attention, including pruning KV Cache [LLC+21, XTC+23] and sparsity-based attention [KKL20, ZHDK23, HJK+23], focus on solving the approximation of the attention matrix, where we call it sparse attention approximation. In particular, we emphasize the importance of stable sparse attention approximation, which directly affects the extensibility of sparse attention under long context scenes. We denote f:ℕ+→ℕ+f:\mathbb{N}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{+} as the strategy to choose a suitable window size due to different input lengths. Hence, we give:

Definition 3.5 (Stable sparse attention approximation 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠⁡(f){\sf SSAA}(f)).

For some strategy f:ℕ+→ℕ+f:\mathbb{N}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{+} to choose the sparsity k=f⁡(n)k=f(n) in sparse attention (Definition 3.4), the problem of stable sparse attention approximation 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠⁡(f){\sf SSAA}(f) is to solve:

L⁡(f,n)=‖Dspar−1​Aspar−D−1​A‖p,\displaystyle L(f,n)=\|D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}-D^{-1}A\|_{p},

where ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} denotes some norm. We say this sparse attention approximation is stable iff:

  • •

    L⁡(f,n)L(f,n) is monotonically decreasing with growing nn.

  • •

    limn→+∞L⁡(f,n)=0\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}L(f,n)=0.

4 Theoretical Insight I: Attention is Provably Naturally Sparse

In this section, we expound on our principal theorem that delineates the sparsity attention, accompanied by a lower limit on ϵ\epsilon. Specifically, the sparsity of attention could be influenced by numerous factors intrinsic to attention computation, such as the length of the context, the weightage assigned to projections of attention, as well as the vector similarity between Query and Key states. Our objective is to identify any inherent principles that shed light on the attention sparsity, consequently aiding the development of efficient attention algorithms.

Initially, we posit that under our assumptions in the previous section, each element in the vector Q​K⊤QK^{\top} is bounded with a high probability, as detailed in Section 4.1. Subsequently, we reinterpret our main problem as a probabilistic problem and give the estimation for ϵ\epsilon to establish the (ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparsity for a given sparsity integer k∈[n]k\in[n] of attention in Section 4.2.

4.1 Concentrations

Before we give our concentration results in attention, firstly, we introduce a key operator in our work, where we conclude that most of the factors influence attention sparsity into one variable. In Definition 4.1, R≥0R\geq 0 is defined by two main factors that may bring negative effects to attention sparsity, where we show as follows:

Definition 4.1.

Denote W:=WQ​WK⊤/d∈ℝd×dW:=W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. We define R:=B2⋅‖W‖FR:=B^{2}\cdot\|W\|_{F}.

Hence, the theoretical concentration results are given below.

Lemma 4.2.

δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). Let R≥0R\geq 0 be defined as Definition 4.1. ∀i1,i2∈[n]\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in[n]. Then with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have

  • •

    Part 1. |(Q​K⊤)i1,i2|≤O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(d/δ)|(QK^{\top})_{i_{1},i_{2}}|\leq O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}.

  • •

    Part 2. exp(−O(R)⋅log⁡(d/δ))≤Ai1,i2≤exp(O(R)⋅log⁡(d/δ))\exp(-O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)})\leq A_{i_{1},i_{2}}\leq\exp(O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}).

  • •

    Part 3. Di1,i1−1≤exp⁡(O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(n​d/δ))/nD_{i_{1},i_{1}}^{-1}\leq\exp(O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(nd/\delta)})/n.

Proof sketch of Lemma 4.2.

Proof of Part 1 follows from the property of inputs XX is bounded, then we apply the Hoeffding inequality (Lemma B.5) to have the results. Proofs of Part 2 and Part 3 are just a simple extension of Part 1 in attention computation. Please refer to Lemma D.4 for the formal proof of Part 1 and refer to Lemma D.3 for the formal proof of Part 2. ∎

Remark. The formal results of Lemma 4.2 in the appendix have slight differences with the informal forms, in which we omit the additional term of each upper bound since such terms are trivially some constants. Fact B.1 shows any constant bias term added before the softmax function will not change the output. We thus simplify the equations for tighter boundaries and more convenient notation. (See Remark D.5)

4.2 Attention Sparsity with Bound on Error

We state our result in Theorem 4.3.

Theorem 4.3.

Let R≥0R\geq 0 be defined as Definition 4.1. Given sparsity integer k≤nk\leq n. Denote T:=exp⁡(log⁡(n⁡(n−k)​d/δ))T:=\exp(\sqrt{\log(n(n-k)d/\delta)}). Let 𝒮ϵ\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon} be defined as Definition 3.2. δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). If we choose ϵ≥TO⁡(R)n\epsilon\geq\frac{T^{O(R)}}{n}, then with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all i∈[n]i\in[n], we have |𝒮ϵ​(Di,i−1​Ai,∗)|≥n−k\Big|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(D^{-1}_{i,i}A_{i,*})\Big|\geq n-k.

Proof sketch of Theorem 4.3.

Follows from Definition 3.2, there is less than kk entries in Di,i−1​Ai,∗∈ℝnD^{-1}_{i,i}A_{i,*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} that are greater than ϵ\epsilon. We can easily get ϵ≥TO⁡(R)n\epsilon\geq\frac{T^{O(R)}}{n} by combining Part 2 and Part 3 of Lemma 4.2. The complete proof is provided in Appendix D and Theorem D.1. ∎

Theorem 4.3 gives the relationship between attention sparsity kk and the error of approximating attention computation by considering only top-kk entries in attention. To our best knowledge, it is the first theoretical analysis that confirms the attention sparsity. It provides a vital framework for our further analysis of sparse attention approximation on exact attention computation. We do not conduct any empirical evaluation for this theorem since this is a trivial finding in the field of efficient attention computations.

5 Theoretical Insight II: Attention Collapse

This section introduces the concept of attention collapse, we formally define it as a phenomenon in attention computation that reveals whatever the values of XX, BB and entries of WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} are (also could be considered as XX and RR), the number of effective entries, whose values are bigger than ϵ\epsilon, in each row of attention matrix, will inevitably decrease to 1 or some constant due to a considerable large input length nn. This result only requires a simple derivation from Theorem D.1, as we show:

Theorem 5.1.

Consider a fixed ϵ\epsilon with a very small value, δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). Then with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, there is:

  • •

    Part 1. If R=o⁡(log⁡(n))R=o(\sqrt{\log(n)}), then we have limn→+∞|𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥n−1\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq n-1.

  • •

    Part 2. If R=O⁡(log⁡(n))R=O(\sqrt{\log(n)}), then we have limn→+∞|𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥O⁡(1)\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq O(1).

Proof sketch of Theorem 5.1.

Consider a fixed ϵ\epsilon with a very small value, |𝒮ϵ​(u)||\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)| could be obtained by n−kn-k, where we have:

|𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥exp⁡(O⁡(log2⁡(ϵ⋅n)R2))⋅δn​d.\displaystyle|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq\exp\Big(O(\frac{\log^{2}(\epsilon\cdot n)}{R^{2}})\Big)\cdot\frac{\delta}{nd}. (1)

Proof sketch of Part 1: Knowing ϵ,δ,R,d\epsilon,\delta,R,d are fixed, this equation will grow hyper-linear with an increasing nn, its maximal is at least n−1n-1 because of some properties of the softmax function. Proof sketch of Part 2: When R=O⁡(log⁡(n))R=O(\sqrt{\log(n)}), the lower bound on |𝒮ϵ​(u)||\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)| is some constant that doesn’t relate to nn. Refer to Theorem D.2 for the detailed proof. ∎

Discussion. Following Theorem D.2, we find that there is a crucial parameter for the attention sparsity, R=B2​‖W‖FR=B^{2}\|W\|_{F}. When R=o⁡(log⁡(n))R=o(\sqrt{\log(n)}) or R=O⁡(log⁡(n))R=O(\sqrt{\log(n)}), which satisfies the bound for most of the situations in current transformer-based models, attention collapse inevitably happens when inputting super-long matrix into attention network. Due to its natural limitation, attention can only focus on a few entries even if we are still inputting more pieces of information, we believe this provides some explanations for several past discoveries, for instance, attention sink [XTC+23], low-rank preserve of attention [CAM+].

Moreover, this theorem can be connected to the fine-grained complexity of attention computation - the bound is astonishingly similar! [AS23] confirm that any fast attention algorithm approximates standard attention within n1+o⁡(1)n^{1+o(1)} executions and 1/poly⁡(n)1/\poly(n) error requires query, key and value state matrices are bounded, mathematically ‖Q‖∞≤o⁡(log⁡(n))\|Q\|_{\infty}\leq o(\sqrt{\log(n)}), ‖K‖∞≤o⁡(log⁡(n))\|K\|_{\infty}\leq o(\sqrt{\log(n)}), ‖V‖∞≤o⁡(log⁡(n))\|V\|_{\infty}\leq o(\sqrt{\log(n)}). Since the ℓF\ell_{F} norm can be transformed into ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm, our results further validate the effectiveness of efficient attention theoretically from the perspective from sparsity.

Experimental Evaluation. Figure 1 indicates the effectiveness of our theory: For a fixed RR, we denote the number of entries that are small than or equal ε\varepsilon in attention matrix as |𝒮ε||{\cal S}_{\varepsilon}|. We sufficiently sample input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} from Gaussian distribution with various input length n∈{21,22,⋯,224}n\in\{2^{1},2^{2},\cdots,2^{24}\}. For different ε∈{1​e−4,5​e−5,2​e−5,1​e−5,⋯,5​e−7,2​e−7,1​e−7}\varepsilon\in\{{\rm 1e-4},5e-5,2e-5,1e-5,\cdots,5e-7,2e-7,1e-7\}, |𝒮ε|/n|{\cal S}_{\varepsilon}|/n inevitably decreases to 0.

6 Theoretical Insight III and IV: On Stable Sparse Attention Approximation

The goal of this section is to explain the success of sparse attention approximation as we defined in Definition 3.5, meanwhile, our analysis indicates an incremental sufficient requirement for stable sparse attention approximation. In detail, we provide the minimum low bound for the window size kk in sparse attention for 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠{\sf SSAA} in Section 6.1. On contrary, we give the lower bound on approximating the error of some common settings in prior works of sparse attention in Section 6.2, which we aim to theoretical support that an invariable kk or even k=o⁡(log⁡(n))k=o(\log(n)) is inappropriate for more efficient stable sparse attention approximation. Finally, in Section 6.3 we conduct experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of our conclusions.

6.1 Theoretical Insight III: Ω⁡(nC)\Omega(n^{C}) Entries Suffice for Stable Sparse Attention Approximation

Based on the attention sparsity framework in Theorem 4.3, we showcase the sufficient bound for 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠{\sf SSAA}, which is:

Theorem 6.1.

δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). For a constant C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1), we then denote f⁡(n):=Ω⁡(nC)f(n):=\Omega(n^{C}), therefore, with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, window size strategy k=f⁡(n)k=f(n) is sufficient to solve 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠⁡(f){\sf SSAA}(f) in Definition 3.5.

Proof sketch of Theorem 6.1.

Recall that L⁡(f,n)=‖Dspar−1​Aspar−D−1​A‖pL(f,n)=\|D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}-D^{-1}A\|_{p} for p=∞p=\infty, we have Dspar−1Aspar−D−1A∥∞≤∥Dspar−1Aspar−D−1Aspar∥∞+∥D−1Aspar−D−1A∥∞D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}-D^{-1}A\|_{\infty}\leq\|D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}-D^{-1}A_{\rm spar}\|_{\infty}+\|D^{-1}A_{\rm spar}-D^{-1}A\|_{\infty}. Thus, these two terms are bounded following Part 1 and Part 4 of Lemma E.3, we can obtain that L⁡(f,n)≤1/nerrorCL(f,n)\leq 1/n^{C}_{\rm error} for a constant Cerror<CC_{\rm error}<C when k=f⁡(n)=nCk=f(n)=n^{C} for a constant C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1). ∎

6.2 Theoretical Insight IV: Sparse Attention Fail to Approximate Exact Attention from o⁡(log⁡(n))o(\log(n)) Entries

Since we provide a sufficient bound for the window size in sparse attention in Theorem 6.1, we also give the insufficient bound which leads the failure of stable sparse attention approximation as follows:

Theorem 6.2.

δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). For a constant C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1), we then denote f⁡(n):=o⁡(log⁡(n))f(n):=o(\log(n)), therefore, with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, window size strategy k=f⁡(n)k=f(n) cannot solve 𝖲𝖲𝖠𝖠⁡(f){\sf SSAA}(f) in Definition 3.5.

Proof sketch of Theorem 6.2.

This proof follows from choosing pp as Frobenius norm and k=o⁡(log⁡(n))k=o(\log(n)), the error function then will be at least monotonically increasing with nn. Please refer to Theorem E.2 for the formal version and corresponding detailed proofs. ∎

Discussion. Theorem 6.1 is an incremental result to theoretically support the existence of attention sparsity. Different from Theorem 4.3, Theorem 6.1 gives the sufficient bound for the number of entries that stable sparse attention approximation requires. Therefore, we ensure that attention computation is at least (ϵ,Ω⁡(nC))(\epsilon,\Omega(n^{C}))-sparse with a very small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. This provides a new perspective on why sparse attention can sometimes be competitive with standard attention. Theorem 6.2 reveals another side of the coin - o⁡(log⁡(n))o(\log(n)) window size is not enough for stable sparse attention approximation, which demonstrates a theoretical perspective for current efficient KV cache methods might still lack scalability towards super-long context length.

6.3 Empirical Evaluation

Setup. This section provides an empirical evaluation of our theoretical results in Section 6.1 and Section 6.2. Here we aim to give some simple examples to confirm our theory. In detail, we simulate the error dynamics of sparse attention approximation within different window size strategies. For instance, we compare the approximating error on attention matrix when k=C1k=C_{1}, k=α1⋅log⁡(n)k=\alpha_{1}\cdot\log(n) and k=α2⋅nC2k=\alpha_{2}\cdot n^{C_{2}}, where C1,C2,α1C_{1},C_{2},\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} are all constants. Specially, we consider a one-layer attention network with WQ=WK=diag⁡(𝟏d)W_{Q}=W_{K}=\diag({\bf 1}_{d}). We choose input length nn from {212,213,⋯,223}\{2^{12},2^{13},\cdots,2^{23}\}. For input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, we sample each entry from Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). We use constant window size as the baseline of this experiment, where kk will be chosen from {128,256,512,1024,2048}\{128,256,512,1024,2048\}. For dynamic window size strategy k=⌊α⋅log⁡(n)⌋k=\lfloor\alpha\cdot\log(n)\rfloor and k=⌊α⋅nC⌋k=\lfloor\alpha\cdot n^{C}\rfloor, we adjust α\alpha to enforce the computational cost is aligned to the cost when applying fixed window size. For example, the computational cost of k=128k=128 is O⁡(∑i=112128​ni)O(\sum_{i=1}^{12}128n_{i}), we compute α1:=∑i=112128​ni/∑i=112log⁡(ni)​ni\alpha_{1}:=\sum_{i=1}^{12}128n_{i}/\sum_{i=1}^{12}\log(n_{i})n_{i} and α2:=∑i=112128​ni/∑i=112ni​ni\alpha_{2}:=\sum_{i=1}^{12}128n_{i}/\sum_{i=1}^{12}\sqrt{n_{i}}n_{i} to satisfy that the compute complexity of k=⌊α1⋅log⁡(n)⌋k=\lfloor\alpha_{1}\cdot\log(n)\rfloor and k=⌊α2⋅n⌋k=\lfloor\alpha_{2}\cdot\sqrt{n}\rfloor equal to O⁡(∑i=112128​ni)O(\sum_{i=1}^{12}128n_{i}). We repeat 1000 times for each setting and take the mean value for the stable and fair result.

Results. As Figure 2 shows, the error of sparse attention approximation with k=Ck=C and k=O⁡(log⁡(n))k=O(\log(n)) window size strategy grows or maintains under the trend of an increasing context length. Meanwhile, window size strategies with nCn^{C} functions perform descents on the error with growing input length nn. Moreover, since the total compute costs are aligned the same for different window size strategies, we validate their mean values of approximating errors and record them in Table 1. As shown, the constant window size strategy performs well, and the k=α​n1/1000k=\alpha n^{1/1000} strategy performs with minimal error, which indicates the dynamic strategy for the window size might be a better choice for the design of advanced sparse attention approaches. We further explore this problem in Section 7.

7 Theoretical Insight V: Dynamic Top-kk Strategy rather than Fixed One

In this section, we aim to develop the more advanced method for stable sparse attention approximation towards the efficient inference tasks of transformer-based models. We first give the theoretical analysis in Section 7.1 and the corresponding empirical evaluation in Section 7.2.

7.1 Theoretical Analysis

We consider a dataset 𝒟:={Xi}i=1N{\cal D}:=\{X^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} with dataset size NN. For all i∈[N]i\in[N], we use nin_{i} to denote the context length, such that Xi∈ℝni×dX^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d}. Hence, the difference of the computational complexities of fixed Top-kk strategy and a dynamic (especially O⁡(nC)O(n^{C})) strategy could be easily obtained in the Claim below.

Claim 7.1.

We have:

  • •

    Part 1. Choosing the constant window size strategy k=pk=p for some constant integer p>0p>0. The computational complexity of a one-layer pp-sparse attention to inference 𝒟={Xi}iN{\cal D}=\{X^{i}\}_{i}^{N} is Θ⁡(p​∑i=1Nni)\Theta(p\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{i}).

  • •

    Part 2. Choosing the constant window size strategy k=α⋅nCk=\alpha\cdot n^{C} for some constant α,C>0\alpha,C>0. The computational complexity of a one-layer pp-sparse attention to inference 𝒟={Xi}iN{\cal D}=\{X^{i}\}_{i}^{N} is Θ⁡(α​∑i=1Nni1+C)\Theta(\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{i}^{1+C}).

Proof.

Recall the computational complexity of Definition 3.4 is O⁡(n​k)O(nk) for input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and kk window size. We then take the summation for each Xi∈ℝni×dX^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d} in 𝒟:={Xi}iN{\cal D}:=\{X^{i}\}_{i}^{N} to obtain the results of Part 1 and Part 2. ∎

Remark. We emphasize the goal of this section is not to present a novel method, in contrast, the design of strategy k=α​nCk=\alpha n^{C} is very careless and retains a lot of room for improvement. However, the proposition we aim to sell in this section, which is: Using dynamic window size strategy rather than fixed window size strategy, the former is provably performs more efficient and higher performance than the latter. We would like provide some simple but constructive insights to help better study the working mechanism behind and better design of sparse attention approximation. As we state below:

Proposition 7.2.

For any window size strategy k=pk=p for some constant integer p>0p>0, there exist a context-length adaptive strategy k=α⋅nCk=\alpha\cdot n^{C} for some constant α,C>0\alpha,C>0 that performs lower approximating error.

Proof.

Following Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 6.2, the conclusion of this proposition can be trivially proved by pluging suitbale choices of α\alpha and CC. ∎

7.2 Evaluation

Setup. In this experiment, we apply k=α​nCk=\alpha n^{C} window size strategy with choosing C=1/1000C=1/1000 and α∈{0.11,0.22}\alpha\in\{0.11,0.22\}. The baseline is set to the classical pruning-KV method, StreamingLLM [XTC+23] with windows sizes k∈{1024,2048}k\in\{1024,2048\} that utilizes attention sink to relieve the bad approximating performance in efficient KV cache approaches. Furthermore, we use the pre-trained model LlaMa-3-8B-Instruct as the backbone of this experiment and we evaluate on the LongBench dataset [BLZ+23]. Especially, each choice of α\alpha here performs less computional time compare to fixed strategies {1024,2048}\{1024,2048\} on LongBench dataset, we thus conduct no additional experiments about computational efficiency in this setting.

Results. The scores of each methods are shown in Table 2 where a greater score represents a better performance for each sub-dataset. As demonstrating, the dynamic window size strategy showcases a strong approximating capability that compares with the fixed window size strategy under the settings k=2048k=2048 and k=1024k=1024. Besides, it also performs a robustness since α\alpha is scaled from 0.220.22 to 0.110.11, the average performance decreases a little. This confirms the correctness of Proposition 7.2 and we believe the potential of this insight for designing future stable sparse attention approximation.

8 Conclusion and Future Discussion

Prior fast algorithms for enhancing the efficiency of language models alleviate the quadratic time complexity of attention computation by assuming attention sparsity, whereas these algorithms lack an appropriate understanding of it. This work provides the first theoretical analysis of attention sparsity, furthermore, our theory leads to an obvious but important conclusion, that is Attention is Provably, Naturally nCn^{C}-Sparse for any constant C∈(0,1)C\in(0,1).

In addition, this analysis of sparsity has brought us several brand-new insights. Here, we re-organize them as takeaways, we hope these can be some solid suggestion for improving future design of transformer-based architectures:

Takeaway 1: It’s necessary to involve a high precision in attention computation to relieve attention collapse. Since the proven concept of attention collapse, meanwhile, a high precision in attention computation means choosing ϵ\epsilon with smaller value in Theorem 5.1, we thus suggest using super-high precision in attention computation to avoid forgetting in the case of long context.

Takeaway 2: A large constant window size for sparse attention approximation is enough, but a dynamic strategy will improve performance. As the results shown in Table 1 and Table 2, fixed window size strategy shows competitive approximating error. We suggest that if the model weights or dataset for inference is unknown to the model developers, using fixed window size strategy will be a insurance and effective method.

At the same time, we discuss two future direction as follows:

Future Direction 1: The upper bound on input and weight matrices (denotes RR in this paper) is vital to attention sparsity, a non-fixed weight, e.g. Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) [SAL+24] might help to address the long-term forgetting. The conclusion of the former sentence is derived from Theorem 5.1. Hence a non-fixed weight (mathematically RR as Definition 4.1) leads to a converging lower bound on the number of ineffective entry in attention matrix. This connects to the long-term extrapolation problem of LLMs, which is a interesting future direction if we utilize the theory of this paper to explain some phenomenons.

Future Direction 2: Context-length and weight-norm adaptive efficient attention. Theorem E.1 shows the importance of context length and weight norm in stable sparse attention approximation. We would like to extend this framework onto general efficient attention computation, providing a novel perspective that is different with fine-grained complexity theory in attention [AS23].

Appendix A More Related Work

To complete the background of the related research, we provide some more related work in this section. The attention mechanism’s computational intensity, particularly within transformer architectures, has been a significant focus, with [DSXY23] delving into the theoretical aspects of data recovery via attention weights. Concurrently, the analysis of softmax attention’s superiority by [DSZ23] and the innovative attention schemes inspired by softmax regression from [DLS23] contribute vital insights into attention mechanism optimization. The discourse extends to the computational frameworks of LLMs, where the theoretical examination of modern Hopfield models by [HLSL24] and the exploration of sparse Hopfield models by [HYW+23] align closely with our research’s objectives. Moreover, the innovative STanHop model by [WHL+24] and the outlier-efficient Hopfield layers presented by [HCL+24] further underscore the burgeoning interest in enhancing computational efficiencies within neural architectures. In parallel, studies on various algorithmic optimizations, such as randomized and deterministic attention sparsification [DMS23b], dynamic kernel sparsifiers [DJS+22], and zero-th order algorithms for softmax attention optimization [DLMS23], provide a comprehensive backdrop to our investigation into attention score sparsity. Further extending the discourse, studies by [XHH+24], [HCW+24], and Wu et al. [WHHL24] delve into novel applications and optimizations of Hopfield networks, showcasing the diverse avenues for computational enhancement in neural network models. [CSY24, CSY23] offer additional perspectives on optimizing LLMs, addressing copyright data protection and fine-tuning for unbiased in-context learning, which underscore the multifaceted challenges in LLM research. The work by [SY23] on learning rate schedules further informs our understanding of model optimization and training efficiency. Moreover, the diverse array of research spanning from Fourier circuits in neural networks [GLL+24], domain generalization [SMF+24], multitask finetuning [XSW+24], to semi-supervised learning frameworks [SSL24, SWL24] and spectral analysis in class discovery [SSLL23] offers a rich backdrop against which our work is situated. The Attention Sink phenomenon, discovered by [XLS+23, BNB24] and is helping to enhance LLMs in [XTC+23, Mil23], is a distinct characteristic commonly observed in most attention networks of LLMs. This phenomenon is characterized by the disproportionate attention these models pay to a specific, often unrelated, token—usually the first token. These tokens are assigned high attention scores, indicating their significant influence within the network. These studies, along with [SCL+23, DLG+22, SWL22, SSL+22] and [QSZZ23, QRS+22, QJS+22, GQSW22, QSZ23, QSW23, QSY23] contributions in algorithmic optimizations and neural network analysis, not only broaden the landscape of our research but also underscore the dynamic and multifaceted nature of computational efficiency and theoretical analysis in the field of LLMs and beyond.

B.4 Probability Tools

Here, we state a probability toolkit in the following, including several helpful lemmas we’d like to use. Firstly, we provide the lemma about Chernoff bound in [Che52] below.

Lemma B.4 (Chernoff bound, [Che52]).

Let X=∑i=1nXiX=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}, where Xi=1X_{i}=1 with probability pip_{i} and Xi=0X_{i}=0 with probability 1−pi1-p_{i}, and all XiX_{i} are independent. Let μ=𝔼[X]=∑i=1npi\mu=\E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}. Then

  • •

    Pr[X≥(1+δ)μ]≤exp(−δ2μ/3)\Pr[X\geq(1+\delta)\mu]\leq\exp(-\delta^{2}\mu/3), ∀δ>0\forall\delta>0;

  • •

    Pr[X≤(1−δ)μ]≤exp(−δ2μ/1)\Pr[X\leq(1-\delta)\mu]\leq\exp(-\delta^{2}\mu/1), ∀0<δ<1\forall 0<\delta<1.

Next, we offer the lemma about Hoeffding bound as in [Hoe94].

Lemma B.5 (Hoeffding bound, [Hoe94]).

Let X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n} denote nn independent bounded variables in [ai,bi][a_{i},b_{i}] for ai,bi∈ℝa_{i},b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}. Let X:=∑i=1nXiX:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}, then we have

Pr[|X−𝔼[X]|≥t]≤2exp(−2​t2∑i=1n(bi−ai)2)\displaystyle\Pr[|X-\E[X]|\geq t]\leq 2\exp(-\frac{2t^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}})

We show the lemma of Bernstein inequality as [Ber24].

Lemma B.6 (Bernstein inequality, [Ber24]).

Let X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n} denote nn independent zero-mean random variables. Suppose |Xi|≤M|X_{i}|\leq M almost surely for all ii. Then, for all positive tt,

Pr[∑i=1nXi≥t]≤exp(−t2/2∑j=1n𝔼[Xj2]+Mt/3)\displaystyle\Pr[\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\geq t]\leq\exp(-\frac{t^{2}/2}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\E[X_{j}^{2}]+Mt/3})

Then, we give the Khintchine’s inequality in [Khi23, Haa81] as follows:

Lemma B.7 (Khintchine’s inequality, [Khi23, Haa81]).

Let σ1,⋯,σn\sigma_{1},\cdots,\sigma_{n} be i.i.d sign random variables, and let z1⋯,znz_{1}\cdots,z_{n} be real numbers. Then there are constants C>0C>0 so that for all t>0t>0

Pr[|∑i=1nziσi|≥t∥z∥2]≤exp(−Ct2)\displaystyle\Pr[|\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}\sigma_{i}|\geq t\|z\|_{2}]\leq\exp(-Ct^{2})

We give Hason-wright inequality from [HW71, RV13] below.

Lemma B.8 (Hason-wright inequality, [HW71, RV13]).

Let x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote a random vector with independent entries xix_{i} with 𝔼[xi]=0\E[x_{i}]=0 and |xi|≤K|x_{i}|\leq K Let AA be an n×nn\times n matrix. Then, for every t≥0t\geq 0

Pr[|x⊤Ax−𝔼[x⊤Ax]|>t]≤2exp(−cmin{t2/(K4∥A∥F2),t/(K2∥A∥)})\displaystyle\Pr[|x^{\top}Ax-\E[x^{\top}Ax]|>t]\leq 2\exp(-c\min\{t^{2}/(K^{4}\|A\|_{F}^{2}),t/(K^{2}\|A\|)\})

We state Lemma 1 on page 1325 of Laurent and Massart [LM00].

Lemma B.9 (Lemma 1 on page 1325 of Laurent and Massart, [LM00]).

Let X∼𝒳k2X\sim\mathcal{X}_{k}^{2} be a chi-squared distributed random variable with kk degrees of freedom. Each one has zero mean and σ2\sigma^{2} variance. Then

Pr[X−kσ2≥(2k​t+2t)σ2]≤exp(−t)\displaystyle\Pr[X-k\sigma^{2}\geq(2\sqrt{kt}+2t)\sigma^{2}]\leq\exp(-t)
Pr[X−kσ2≥2k​tσ2]≤exp(−t)\displaystyle\Pr[X-k\sigma^{2}\geq 2\sqrt{kt}\sigma^{2}]\leq\exp(-t)

Here, we provide a tail bound for sub-exponential distribution [FKZ+11].

Lemma B.10 (Tail bound for sub-exponential distribution, [FKZ+11]).

We say X∈SE⁡(σ2,α)X\in\mathrm{SE}(\sigma^{2},\alpha) with parameters σ>0\sigma>0, α>0\alpha>0, if

𝔼[eλ​X]≤exp⁡(λ2​σ2/2),∀|λ|<1/α.\displaystyle\E[e^{\lambda X}]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}/2),\forall|\lambda|<1/\alpha.

Let X∈SE⁡(σ2,α)X\in\mathrm{SE}(\sigma^{2},\alpha) and 𝔼[X]=μ\E[X]=\mu, then:

Pr[|X−μ|≥t]≤exp(−0.5min{t2/σ2,t/α})\displaystyle\Pr[|X-\mu|\geq t]\leq\exp(-0.5\min\{t^{2}/\sigma^{2},t/\alpha\})

In the following, we show the helpful lemma of matrix Chernoff bound as in [Tro11, LDFU13].

Lemma B.11 (Matrix Chernoff bound, [Tro11, LDFU13]).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a finite set of positive-semidefinite matrices with dimension d×dd\times d, and suppose that

maxX∈𝒳⁡λmax​(X)≤B.\displaystyle\max_{X\in\mathcal{X}}\lambda_{\rm max}(X)\leq B.

Sample {X1,⋯,Xn}\{X_{1},\cdots,X_{n}\} uniformly at random from 𝒳\mathcal{X} without replacement. We define μmin\mu_{\rm min} and μmax\mu_{\rm max} as follows:

μmin:=n⋅λmin​(𝔼X∈𝒳(X))\displaystyle\mu_{\rm min}:=n\cdot\lambda_{\rm min}(\E_{X\in\mathcal{X}}(X))
μmax:=n⋅λmax​(𝔼X∈𝒳(X)).\displaystyle\mu_{\rm max}:=n\cdot\lambda_{\rm max}(\E_{X\in\mathcal{X}}(X)).

Then

Pr[λmin(∑i=1nXi)≤(1−δ)μmin]≤d⋅exp(−δ2μmin/B) for δ∈(0,1],\displaystyle~\Pr[\lambda_{\rm min}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i})\leq(1-\delta)\mu_{\rm min}]\leq d\cdot\exp(-\delta^{2}\mu_{\rm min}/B)\text{~for~}\delta\in(0,1],
Pr[λmax(∑i=1nXi)≥(1+δ)μmax]≤d⋅exp(−δ2μmax/(4B)) for δ≥0.\displaystyle~\Pr[\lambda_{\rm max}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i})\geq(1+\delta)\mu_{\rm max}]\leq d\cdot\exp(-\delta^{2}\mu_{\rm max}/(4B))\text{~for~}\delta\geq 0.

Appendix C Problem Definitions

C.1 Input Assumption

Definition C.1.

We consider for any input matrix to an attention network X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} where integer nn denotes the input length and dd denotes the dimension. We assume:

  • •

    Independent Entries. For any two entries Xi1,j1X_{i_{1},j_{1}} and Xi2,j2X_{i_{2},j_{2}} in matrix XX, ∀i1,i2∈[n]\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in[n] and j1,j2∈[d]j_{1},j_{2}\in[d], they are independent.

  • •

    Bounded Entries. For failure probability δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1). With a probability 1−δ1-\delta, the entry Xi,jX_{i,j} in matrix XX, ∀i∈[n]\forall i\in[n] and j∈[d]j\in[d], we have |Xi,j|≤B|X_{i,j}|\leq B for some positive constant B>0B>0.

C.2 Attention Computation

Definition C.2 (Attention computation).

If the following conditions hold:

  • •

    Let WQ,WK,WV∈ℝd×dW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be denoted as Query, Key and Value projection matrices of attention.

  • •

    Given an input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} that holds properties in Definition C.1.

  • •

    Define Query, Key and Value states matrices Q:=X​WQ,K:=X​WK,V:=X​WV∈ℝn×dQ:=XW_{Q},K:=XW_{K},V:=XW_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

  • •

    A:=exp⁡(Q​K⊤/d)∈ℝn×nA:=\exp(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

  • •

    D:=diag⁡(A​𝟏n)∈ℝn×nD:=\diag(A{\bf 1}_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

Then we have attention computation 𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V)∈ℝn×d{\sf Attn}(Q,K,V)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} as follows:

𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V):=D−1​A​V\displaystyle{\sf Attn}(Q,K,V):=D^{-1}AV

C.3 ϵ\epsilon-Approximated kk-Sparse Softmax Vector

In order to describe the sparsity of the softmax, we define the following notation.

Definition C.3.

For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, we define sparse set 𝒮ϵ​(u)\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u) as follows:

𝒮ϵ​(u):={i∈[n]||ui|≤ϵ}\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u):=\Big\{i\in[n]~\Big|~|u_{i}|\leq\epsilon\Big\}
Definition C.4 ((ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparsity).

For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we say uu is (ϵ,k)(\epsilon,k)-sparse if for a constant ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), it holds that

|𝒮ϵ​(u)|≥n−k.\displaystyle|\mathcal{S}_{\epsilon}(u)|\geq n-k.

C.4 Sparse Attention

Definition C.5.

For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Given a sparsity integer kk. Let 𝒮ϵ{\cal S}_{\epsilon} be defined as Definition C.3 for some error ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We define the top-kk set 𝒯k​(u):={i∈[n]|𝒮ui​(u)≥n−k}{\cal T}_{k}(u):=\{i\in[n]~|~{\cal S}_{u_{i}}(u)\geq n-k\}.

Definition C.6.

If the following conditions hold:

  • •

    For a vector u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  • •

    Given a sparsity integer kk.

  • •

    Let 𝒮ϵ{\cal S}_{\epsilon} be defined as Definition C.3 for some error ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

  • •

    Denote a top-kk set 𝒯k​(u):={i∈[n]|𝒮ui​(u)≥n−k}{\cal T}_{k}(u):=\{i\in[n]~|~{\cal S}_{u_{i}}(u)\geq n-k\} as Definition C.5.

Then we define

𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(u):=[ui⋅𝟏i∈𝒯k​(u)]i∈[n]∈ℝn\displaystyle{\sf topk}(u):=[u_{i}\cdot{\bf 1}_{i\in{\cal T}_{k}(u)}]_{i\in[n]}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

We define the sparse attention computation as follows:

Definition C.7.

If the following conditions hold:

  • •

    Let WQ,WK,WV∈ℝd×dW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be denoted as Query, Key and Value projection matrices of attention.

  • •

    Given an input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} that holds properties in Definition C.1.

  • •

    Define Query, Key and Value states matrices Q:=X​Z​WQ,K:=X​WK,V:=X​WV∈ℝn×dQ:=XZW_{Q},K:=XW_{K},V:=XW_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

  • •

    A:=exp⁡(Q​K⊤/d)∈ℝn×nA:=\exp(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

  • •

    Let 𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄{\sf topk} be defined as Definition C.6.

  • •

    Define Aspar:=[𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(A1),𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(A2),⋯,𝗍𝗈𝗉𝗄⁡(An)]⊤∈ℝn×nA_{\rm spar}:=\begin{bmatrix}{\sf topk}(A_{1}),&{\sf topk}(A_{2}),&\cdots,&{\sf topk}(A_{n})\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

  • •

    Dspar:=diag⁡(Aspar​𝟏n)∈ℝn×nD_{\rm spar}:=\diag(A_{\rm spar}{\bf 1}_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

  • •

    δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1).

  • •

    Let R≥0R\geq 0 be defined as Definition C.9.

The sparse attention computation 𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V)∈ℝn×d{\sf SparseAttn}(Q,K,V)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is given by:

𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇⁡(Q,K,V):=Dspar−1​Aspar​V∈ℝn×d\displaystyle{\sf SparseAttn}(Q,K,V):=D_{\rm spar}^{-1}A_{\rm spar}V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}

Proof of Part 1. We have

|A~i1,i2|=\displaystyle|\widetilde{A}_{i_{1},i_{2}}|= exp⁡((Q​K⊤)i1,i2)\displaystyle~\exp((QK^{\top})_{i_{1},i_{2}})

D.4 Concentration on Q​K⊤QK^{\top}

Lemma D.4.

If the following conditions hold:

  • •

    Let WQ,WK,WV∈ℝd×dW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be denoted as Query, Key and Value projection matrices of attention.

  • •

    Given an input X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} that holds properties in Definition C.1.

  • •

    Define Query, Key and Value states matrices Q:=X​WQ,K:=X​WK,V:=X​WV∈ℝn×dQ:=XW_{Q},K:=XW_{K},V:=XW_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}.

  • •

    Let W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be define as Definition C.8.

  • •

    Denote C≥1C\geq 1 as a sufficient large constant.

  • •

    δ∈(0,0.1)\delta\in(0,0.1).

  • •

    Let R≥0R\geq 0 be defined as Definition C.9.

  • •

    For i1,i2∈[n]i_{1},i_{2}\in[n]

Then with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have

|(Q​K⊤)i1,i2|≤O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(d/δ)+βi2\displaystyle|(QK^{\top})_{i_{1},i_{2}}|\leq O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}+\beta_{i_{2}}
Proof.

We have:

|(Q​K⊤)i1,i2|=\displaystyle|(QK^{\top})_{i_{1},i_{2}}|= |(X​WQ​WK⊤​X⊤/d)i1,i2|\displaystyle~|(XW_{Q}W_{K}^{\top}X^{\top}/\sqrt{d})_{i_{1},i_{2}}|
=\displaystyle= |(X​W​X⊤)i1,i2|\displaystyle~|(XWX^{\top})_{i_{1},i_{2}}|
=\displaystyle= |Xi1⊤​W​Xi2|\displaystyle~|X_{i_{1}}^{\top}WX_{i_{2}}|
=\displaystyle= |∑j1=1d∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi1,j1​Xi2,j2|\displaystyle~|\sum_{j_{1}=1}^{d}\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{1},j_{1}}X_{i_{2},j_{2}}|
≤\displaystyle\leq B​|∑j1=1d∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2|\displaystyle~B|\sum_{j_{1}=1}^{d}\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}|

where the first step follows from Q:=X​WQ,K:=X​WKQ:=XW_{Q},K:=XW_{K}, the second step follows from Definition C.9, the third and fourth steps follow from simple algebras, the fifth step follows from Definition C.1.

We then apply Hoeffding inequality (Lemma B.5) to each Wj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}. Hence, with a probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have:

|∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2−𝔼[∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2]|≤\displaystyle|\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}-\E[\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}]|\leq O⁡(B)⋅‖Wj1‖2⋅log⁡(d/δ)\displaystyle~O(B)\cdot\|W_{j_{1}}\|_{2}\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}

since |Xi2,j2|≤B|X_{i_{2},j_{2}}|\leq B for any j2∈[d]j_{2}\in[d].

By triangle inequality, we have:

|∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2|≤\displaystyle|\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}|\leq O⁡(B)⋅‖Wj1‖2⋅log⁡(d/δ)+|𝔼[∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2]|\displaystyle~O(B)\cdot\|W_{j_{1}}\|_{2}\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}+|\E[\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}]| (5)

We obtain:

B​|∑j1=1d∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2|≤\displaystyle B|\sum_{j_{1}=1}^{d}\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}|\leq O⁡(B2)⋅‖W‖F⋅log⁡(d/δ)+B​d​maxj1∈[d]​|𝔼[∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2]|\displaystyle~O(B^{2})\cdot\|W\|_{F}\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}+Bd\max_{j_{1}\in[d]}|\E[\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}]|
=\displaystyle= O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(d/δ)+βi2\displaystyle~O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(d/\delta)}+\beta_{i_{2}}

where the first step follows from Eq 5 and Fact B.2 (‖W‖F=∑j1=1d‖Wj1‖22\|W\|_{F}=\sum_{j_{1}=1}^{d}\|W_{j_{1}}\|_{2}^{2}), the second step follows from Definition C.9 and define

βi2:=B​d​maxj1∈[d]​|𝔼[∑j2=1dWj1,j2⋅Xi2,j2]|\displaystyle\beta_{i_{2}}:=Bd\max_{j_{1}\in[d]}|\E[\sum_{j_{2}=1}^{d}W_{j_{1},j_{2}}\cdot X_{i_{2},j_{2}}]|

∎

Remark D.5.

The formal results of Lemma D.4 in the appendix have slight differences with the informal forms, in which we omit the additional terms of each upper bound since such terms are trivially some constants. Fact B.1 shows any constant bias term added before the softmax function will not change the output. We thus simplify the equations for tighter boundaries and more convenient notation.

‖Dspar−1−D−1‖∞=\displaystyle\|D_{\rm spar}^{-1}-D^{-1}\|_{\infty}= ‖Dspar−1‖∞⋅‖D−1‖∞⋅‖Dspar−D‖∞\displaystyle~\|D_{\rm spar}^{-1}\|_{\infty}\cdot\|D^{-1}\|_{\infty}\cdot\|D_{\rm spar}-D\|_{\infty}

≤\displaystyle\leq n−kn​k⋅exp⁡(O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(n​d/δ))⋅exp⁡(O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(n​d/δ))\displaystyle~\frac{n-k}{nk}\cdot\exp(O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(nd/\delta)})\cdot\exp(O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(nd/\delta)})
≤\displaystyle\leq n−kn​k⋅exp⁡(O⁡(R)⋅log⁡(n​d/δ))\displaystyle~\frac{n-k}{nk}\cdot\exp(O(R)\cdot\sqrt{\log(nd/\delta)})

where the first step follows from simple algebras, the second step follows from Part 2 of this Lemma, the third step follows from Part 5 and Part 6 of Lemma E.4, the last step follows from Eq. (7).

Proof of Part 4. This proof follows from combining Part 2 of Lemma E.4 and Part 3 of this Lemma. ∎
